# Artifacts: pages an agent publishes for people

An artifact is one page that people of your organisation open on LakehouseBox: a dashboard, a report, a map. You publish its HTML and name the catalogs it reads. The page holds no data: its script reads the tables live, in the browser of whoever opens it, with that person's own permissions.

```
lhbox artifact publish garden.html --title "The garden, last 14 days" --catalog garden   # a new page: prints its address
lhbox artifact ls                                                # the artifacts this key can see
lhbox artifact pull a_z1lgMWNSby3J9iOsUiFdGw garden-page         # its files into a folder, to change them
lhbox artifact publish garden-page --note "Added soil moisture"  # the next version of the same page
```

A new artifact is private to the person behind the key that published it. The person: opens the address the publish printed, and shares the page from there if others should see it. An agent never shares a page.

## Writing the page

The page is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. It loads one module, the runtime, from the page's own host:

```
<!doctype html>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<title>Readings</title>
<h1>Readings, last 14 days</h1>
<div id="total">Loading…</div>
<script type="module">
import { lhbox } from '/_lhbox/lhbox.js';
lhbox.panel(document.getElementById('total'), async (el) => {
  const { rows } = await lhbox.query(
    "SELECT count(*) AS n FROM garden.main.readings WHERE ts > now() - INTERVAL 14 DAY");
  el.textContent = rows[0].n + ' readings';
});
</script>
```

| call | what it does |
|---|---|
| lhbox.query(sql, {params}) | Runs one DuckDB statement in the viewer's browser and answers {columns, rows}. columns is a list of {name, type}, in the statement's order, with a DuckDB type name such as bigint, double, varchar, date, timestamp or decimal(18,3). Each row is an object keyed by column name. params fills the ? marks of a prepared statement. |
| lhbox.panel(element, fn) | Runs fn(element). When the viewer cannot read a catalog the function queries, the element shows a note naming it, such as "You can't read garden", and the rest of the page keeps working. |
| lhbox.duckdb() | The engine's connection with the catalogs attached, for Arrow results and prepared statements. |
| lhbox.asset(path) | The address of one of the artifact's own files that loads now. Use it for a file fetched late, such as an image shown on a click. |
| lhbox.open(url) | Asks LakehouseBox to open a link. The person sees the address and confirms before a new tab opens. |
| lhbox.download(name, data) | Offers a file the page made, such as a CSV of a result: data is a Blob, a string or bytes, at most 25 MB. The person sees the file's name and size and confirms before it is saved. Answers a promise: true once saved. |
| lhbox.copy(text) | Puts text on the clipboard, at most 1 MB. Call it from a click or a key press. Answers a promise: true once copied. |
| lhbox.setState(text, {push}), lhbox.onState(fn), lhbox.state | The page's own place (a view, a filter, a selection) as one string of at most 2,000 characters, kept in the address of the page around it, so a reload, a copied link and Back return to it. setState replaces the address; {push: true} adds a step to the browser's history. onState(fn) hears the address change (Back, Forward, a link) and returns a function that stops it. lhbox.state is the place the page was opened at, once lhbox.ready() has resolved (below). |
| lhbox.link | The address that opens this page at its current place, for a "copy link" button: lhbox.copy(lhbox.link). For a private page or one shared with the organisation it is the page's address in the account, https://lakehousebox.com/app/#artifact=<id>&s=<state>; for a public page, the public page's address, https://lakehousebox.com/app/a/public-page?<id>#s=<state>. Without a state, the part from &s= or #s= is left out. It follows setState, Back and Forward, and a change of the page's sharing. It never grants access: whoever opens it signs in, or opens the public page, and sees what they may read. |
| lhbox.ready() | A promise that resolves with lhbox once LakehouseBox has answered the page, with lhbox.state and lhbox.link set. It rejects with code: 'no_viewer' when the page is opened by itself, outside LakehouseBox. |
| lhbox.engine | The engine the page runs: duckdb-wasm-2.0.0, or duckdb-wasm-1.5.6 for a version published before 13 November 2026 (below). |
| lhbox.catalogs, lhbox.unreadable, lhbox.viewer | The catalogs attached, the ones this viewer cannot read with the reason, and the viewer's name. |

- Name tables catalog.namespace.table, as in lhbox query and the MCP query tool. Test each statement there first: the same SQL runs in the page. Another organisation's public catalog <handle>/<catalog> is read as <handle>_<catalog>.namespace.table.

- Wrap every chart, table and number in lhbox.panel. Never assume the viewer reads what you read.

- Aggregate in SQL and return what the page draws. A phone opens this page: thousands of rows, not millions.

- Show the title and the layout at once, and fill the panels as the queries answer. The engine starts on the first query.

- Nothing is cached between calls. Keep a result in a variable to use it twice.

- Values arrive ready for JSON. A timestamp is an ISO 8601 string in UTC and a date is YYYY-MM-DD. A 64-bit integer or a decimal that does not fit a number exactly is a string.

- A page laid out to the window, such as a full-screen map, says <meta name="lhbox-layout" content="fill">.

- Inside the frame, location.hash is not the address people see or share. A page with views of its own keeps its place with lhbox.setState and reads it back from lhbox.state and lhbox.onState.

- lhbox.state and lhbox.link are empty until lhbox.ready() resolves. A page that reads them as the module loads never opens at the linked place (the console says so). Wait for the answer first: const { state } = await lhbox.ready(); showView(state); lhbox.onState(showView);

- The frame cannot save files or reach the clipboard by itself (a link with download, navigator.clipboard): use lhbox.download and lhbox.copy.

## The engine

The page's SQL runs in DuckDB 2.0.0, compiled to WebAssembly, in the viewer's browser. A version keeps the engine it was published with: versions published before 13 November 2026 run DuckDB 1.5.6, and publishing the page again moves it to 2.0.0. Both read the same tables with the same SQL. A query over many files of a partitioned table is the one you will notice: on a page that reads a year-partitioned table of 39 files, that query took about 1 s on 2.0.0 against 3 s on 1.5.6 (Chromium; measured 13 November 2026).

## Time

The page's engine runs in UTC, as the query tools do, so the same statement answers the same in both. now() - INTERVAL 14 DAY, date_trunc('day', ts), ts::DATE and strftime(ts, …) work on a TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE column, and a day is a UTC day for every viewer.

For the viewer's own time, say so in the page: ts AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Madrid' in SQL, or format the ISO string in JavaScript with new Date(value).toLocaleString().

Two forms never depend on the session's zone, if you prefer them: a literal bound, ts > TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-10-29 00:00:00+00', and the day number, epoch_ms(ts) // 86400000.

## What the page can reach

The page runs in a sandboxed frame on a host of its own, apart from the account page.

| it can | it cannot |
|---|---|
| read the catalogs it names, as the viewer | read a catalog it did not name, or one the viewer cannot read |
| load its own files and assets, fonts included | send a request to any other host: no fetch, no external images or fonts |
| load a script or a stylesheet from cdnjs.cloudflare.com, cdn.jsdelivr.net or unpkg.com | load a script from anywhere else |
| draw with inline SVG, canvas, CSS and its own JavaScript | use cookies, storage, forms or popups, or leave its frame |
| show basemap tiles from tiles.lakehousebox.com | see anything of the account page or the viewer's session |

A font is an asset: put the .woff2 file in assets/ and name it in the page's CSS as @font-face { font-family: 'Source Sans 3'; src: url(../assets/source-sans-3-400.woff2) format('woff2'); }. Fonts from Google Fonts or any other host are blocked.

Put nothing private in the HTML. Whoever the page is shared with can read its source, so no secret, no copied rows and no personal data belong in the file. Data stays in the tables, and each viewer sees only what they may read.

## Publishing

Name every catalog the page's SQL reads. You can only name catalogs you read as a whole: a grant on some namespaces or tables is refused, and so is a catalog your key was not given.

| from | how |
|---|---|
| the CLI | lhbox artifact publish PAGE --title TEXT --catalog CATALOG: one HTML file, or a folder |
| the API | POST /v1/artifacts with {"title", "catalogs", "html"} publishes in one call |
| an MCP host | the publish_artifact tool, with read_artifact and list_artifacts |
| a hosted agent | the same three tools, when its definition has artifacts |

A page of several files is a folder: page/ holds index.html and the other page files, assets/ holds images, fonts and other binary files, and the page refers to an asset as ../assets/<name>. lhbox artifact pull writes that folder and lhbox artifact publish <folder> publishes it back as the next version. A folder published as a new artifact gets an artifact.json too, with the artifact's id and catalogs, so publishing the same folder again makes its next version, not a second artifact.

An asset is stored under the SHA-256 of its content (assets/<sha256>.woff2), and the publish rewrites each assets/<name> in the page files to that stored name. A pulled page therefore does not match its source file for file: compare the page with your source after replacing the stored names, or keep the source as the one you edit.

Over the API a folder is three steps. POST /v1/artifacts without html starts a pending version. Each file goes up with PUT /v1/artifacts/{id}/versions/{version}/files/{name}. POST /v1/artifacts/{id}/versions/{version}/publish shows it. Nothing is shown until that last call answers.

## Versions

To change a page, publish its next version: pass artifact_id to the API and the MCP tool, or --artifact to the CLI. With --artifact and no --catalog, the CLI names the catalogs the artifact reads now.

- A version is the whole page. What you do not send is not in it, except the artifact's assets, which a version sent in one call goes on naming.

- Read the page before you change it: lhbox artifact pull, the read_artifact tool, or GET /v1/artifacts/{id}/files, which answers the page files as text. A file marked truncated or omitted is not the whole file: do not publish a version built from it. lhbox artifact pull always writes every file whole.

- Add a note, one line saying what changed: --note, or "note" in the body. People see it in the list of versions.

- One page per subject. Keep it current with new versions instead of publishing a second page.

- A key or an MCP connection publishes versions of the artifacts it made. A hosted agent publishes versions of the ones it keeps (below). A person publishes versions of theirs and of the ones their agents made. Anyone else is refused.

## Who sees it

- A new artifact is private: only the person it belongs to opens it.

- The person shares it on the page itself: with named members of the organisation, with the whole organisation, or with anyone on the internet (below). An agent's key, an MCP connection and a hosted agent cannot share, delete or duplicate an artifact.

- Sharing lets someone open the page. It gives them no data: a viewer who does not read a catalog sees a note such as "You can't read garden" in the panels that query it. The Share panel says so for each person before they are added.

- A page is opened by a person signed in on the account page. An API key cannot open one.

## Making a page public

A public page is opened by anyone on the internet, with no account, at its public link. Around the page we show its title, the organisation that published it, Use this in your account, Get started and Report, and Follow where its owner lets visitors subscribe to the page's agent. Search engines are asked not to index it.

Public pages are turned on per organisation. Where they are on, the Share panel's General access offers Anyone on the internet.

- Only the page's owner makes it public, signed in on the account page (asked to confirm it is them when they signed in more than 12 hours ago). A key, an MCP connection and a hosted agent cannot, and neither can an admin for someone else's page.

- The owner needs a verified address, and the organisation's setting for publishing catalogs has to let them publish: admins by default.

- A public page reads public catalogs only. If the page names a private catalog, the panel lists it with its tables and its size, and making the page public makes that catalog public too. Anyone on the internet can then read and copy every table of it, not only what the page shows. You confirm each catalog by typing its name.

- A public page keeps only the version it shows. Its earlier versions are deleted when it becomes public, and each new version replaces the one before. Whoever opens the page can read its files, so put nothing in them you would not publish.

- An organisation makes at most 10 pages public a day.

- While a page is public, a version that names a catalog which is not public is refused with 409 artifact_public_private_data. An agent goes on publishing versions of a public page under that rule.

- If a catalog is made private again while a public page reads it, visitors see "This catalog is no longer public" in the panels that query it, and the owner is told on the page.

Making the page private again takes it off the web at once. The panel then offers to make private the catalogs that going public had published, and no others.

A page stops being public when it is deleted, when its owner leaves the organisation, and when public pages are turned off for the organisation. A restored page is private.

Making a page public is also where its owner decides whether visitors may subscribe to its agent's updates: Letting visitors follow a page.

| over the API |  |
|---|---|
| PATCH /v1/artifacts/{id} with {"sharing": "public", "dry_run": true} | answers the plan: each catalog, and for a private one its tables, its size and the name to confirm |
| PATCH /v1/artifacts/{id} with {"sharing": "public", "confirm_catalogs": {"<warehouse id>": "<name>"}} | makes it public, from a browser session |
| PATCH /v1/artifacts/{id} with {"sharing": "private", "unpublish_catalogs": ["<warehouse id>"]} | makes it private, and those catalogs with it |
| GET /v1/artifacts/{id} | public_url, and for its owner public.copies |
| PATCH /v1/artifacts/{id} with {"follow": true, "follow_ack": {"catalogs": ["<warehouse id>"], "integrations": false}} | lets visitors subscribe to the page's agent, from a browser session; {"follow": false} stops it |

### Use this in your account

A visitor who is signed in, or who signs in or signs up from the public page, gets a private copy of the page in their own organisation. The copy reads the same public catalogs under the same names, so it works at once, and it says where it came from. Nothing but the page is copied. The owner of the original sees how many copies were made. Over the API it is POST /v1/artifacts/{id}/duplicate on a public page, with {"org_id"} to choose the organisation.

### Reports

Report on a public page sends us what the visitor says is wrong with it. We can take a page off the web. Its owner then sees that it was taken down and why, and cannot make it public again until we lift that.

### Letting visitors follow a page

A visitor of a public page can subscribe by email to what the page's agent writes about it. They follow the agent, for that page: its updates, and the note of each version it publishes.

The page's owner decides, and it is off until they turn it on. The choice is offered when the page is made public and afterwards in the Share panel, and only for a page that has an agent.

Nobody reads an update before it is emailed. Not the owner, and not us. So before the owner says yes, the panel names what the agent reads that is not public: the private catalogs it reads or has read, and whether it uses a person's connected accounts. What the agent writes may carry what it read there. If the agent is later given another private catalog, the emails stop until the owner confirms again.

- Only the owner turns it on, signed in on the account page, after a recent sign-in. A key, an agent and an admin cannot. The owner or an admin turns it off.

- Turning it off stops the emails at once and keeps the list. So does making the page private, giving the page to another agent or taking it from its agent, and a takedown. The owner turns it on again on purpose.

- The emails also stop while public pages are turned off for the organisation.

- Deleting the page deletes the addresses. A restored page has none.

- The owner sees how many people subscribed and the last things the agent said. The owner never sees an address.

- A page takes at most 200 subscribers.

For a visitor:

- Follow asks for an email address. We send one email with a link to confirm it. Nothing else is sent to an address until that link is followed.

- Every email has the page's link, the organisation that published it, "Made with LakehouseBox" and a link to unsubscribe. Mail apps that show an unsubscribe button use the same link.

- Unsubscribing erases the address from the page's list.

- No account is made.

The answer to a subscription is always the same, whether the page takes subscribers or not and whether the address is already subscribed. An address is sent at most one confirmation per page a day and three a week.

| over the API |  |
|---|---|
| GET /v1/artifacts/{id} | follow: on, live, and for the owner agent, agent_reads, subscribers, updates |
| PATCH /v1/artifacts/{id} with {"follow": true, "follow_ack": {...}} | turns it on. follow_ack repeats follow.agent_reads: the ids of its catalogs and its integrations. 400 confirmation_required carries what the agent reads now |
| POST /v1/a/{id}/open | follow: {"agent": "<name>"} when visitors may subscribe, else null |
| POST /v1/a/{id}/subscribe with {"email": "<address>"} | no account needed; always 202 |

## A hosted agent that keeps a page

A hosted agent (https://lakehousebox.com/docs/hosted-agents/) whose definition has artifacts gets publish_artifact, read_artifact, list_artifacts and post_update. A new agent has it; turn it on for an older one with lhbox agent update <name> --artifacts.

- A page the agent publishes is private and belongs to the person who created the agent.

- The agent reads and updates the pages it keeps: the ones it published and the ones it was given. It lists those and no others.

- The person who owns a page gives it to an agent they manage on the page's menu, or with PATCH /v1/artifacts/{id} and {"agent": "<agent name>"}. The answer names the page's catalogs that agent cannot read: it cannot publish a version that reads them until it is given the catalog.

- The person takes a page back the same way ({"agent": null}), or gives it to another agent. From then the agent that kept it no longer lists, reads or updates it (404 artifact_not_found), even when it made the page. It can still publish a new page: to stop that, change its task or turn its artifacts off (lhbox agent update <name> --no-artifacts).

- A run publishes at most 5 versions. A test run checks the page and publishes nothing.

- post_update says one short thing about a page the agent keeps: plain text, at most 600 characters, no link or address. It goes to the people who already get the agent's notices, as one of its notices of the day (it leaves the run's own notice free). Where the page's owner lets visitors follow the page, it is also emailed to the page's subscribers, as written. At most one update per page in a run, 3 in a run and 2 per page a day. A test run posts nothing.

- The agent publishes one self-contained HTML file. It cannot update a page made of several page files, and its version never renames the page: the title is its owner's.

- The agent's own access decides what its pages show. When the agent is deleted, or loses a catalog, the pages it published last show no data from that catalog. The person who owns the page re-owns it from the note the page shows, and it reads what they read.

## When it fails

| error | what it wants |
|---|---|
| 403 artifact_needs_catalog_read | You hold only namespaces or tables of a catalog the page names. Ask an admin for read on the catalog, or leave it out. |
| 403 forbidden, 404 warehouse_not_found, 403 connection_not_granted | A catalog the page names is not one this key reads. Name a catalog you read, or have the person give this key the catalog. |
| 403 artifact_not_yours | The artifact was published by someone else. Publish a new one, or have its owner publish the version. |
| 404 artifact_not_found | No artifact you can see has that id. lhbox artifact ls lists yours. |
| 403 claim_required | The organisation was made without an account. The person keeps it first: lhbox claim. |
| 409 artifact_limit | The organisation keeps 200 artifacts. Publish a version of an existing one, or have the person delete one. |
| 413 artifact_too_large | A page file is over 2 MB, an asset over 20 MB, or the version over 25 MB. Read the data from a table instead of shipping it. |
| 415 artifact_type_refused | The file type is not one an artifact holds. See the limits below. |
| 429 rate_limited | More than 30 versions in an hour from one key. Publish when the content changes, not on a timer. |
| 429 artifact_publish_limit | A hosted agent's run published its 5 versions. |
| 409 artifact_several_files | A hosted agent tried to update a page made of several files. Its owner updates it with lhbox artifact publish <folder>. |
| 403 public_artifacts_not_enabled | Public pages are not turned on for the organisation. |
| 400 confirmation_required | Making the page public would make a private catalog public. Send its name in confirm_catalogs; the answer lists what is missing. |
| 409 artifact_public_private_data | A public page reads public catalogs only. Name public catalogs, or have the owner make the page private first. |
| 403 artifact_public_blocked | We took the page off the web. It cannot be made public again until that is lifted. |
| 403 address_not_verified | The owner's address is not verified yet. |
| 403 artifacts_not_allowed | The hosted agent's definition does not have artifacts. Whoever manages it turns it on. |
| http_499 with no message from an upload | The connection closed before an answer came: a timeout or a reset on the way. On a CI runner whose uploads hang, run sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing=1 on the runner first, then publish again. |

## Numbers and dates

| limit | value |
|---|---|
| page files | .html .css .js .json .geojson .csv .svg, at most 2 MB each |
| assets | .png .jpg .jpeg .webp .gif .avif .woff2 .parquet .pmtiles .mp4, at most 20 MB each |
| one version | at most 25 MB and 200 files |
| catalogs a page names | at most 20 |
| versions kept | the newest 20 |
| a note | cut at 200 characters |
| publishing | 30 versions an hour for each key; a hosted agent's run 5 |
| reading a page's files back | 60 an hour for each key |
| artifacts in an organisation | 200 |
| a deleted artifact | restorable by the person for 7 days |
| lhbox.download | 25 MB a file |
| lhbox.copy | 1 MB of text |
| lhbox.setState | 2,000 characters |

Measured on 12 November 2026 on DuckDB 1.5.6, in Chromium and WebKit: loading the engine's time-zone support adds about 0.1 s to the first query and 1.6 MB to the first open in a browser. On 2.0.0 it is about 0.04 s and 0.7 MB (13 November 2026).
